concept.name: Day trading
concept.definition: A speculative trading approach in which a trader buys and sells (or sells and buys) the same financial instrument within the same trading day, closing all positions before the session ends to avoid overnight gap risk. Under FINRA rules, a 'day trade' is the purchase and sale of the same security on the same day in a margin account, and customers executing four or more day trades in five business days are designated pattern day traders subject to special margin requirements.
concept.intuition: Day traders try to profit from intraday price swings, riding a stock's momentum for seconds to hours, and never hold positions overnight.
concept.mechanics: Positions are opened and closed during a single session, often on margin and with direct-access platforms; true day traders hold nothing overnight. In U.S. margin accounts, pattern day traders must maintain at least $25,000 in equity and are subject to day-trading buying-power limits.
concept.failure_modes: High leverage, commissions, and spread costs cause most retail day traders to lose money; academic studies of day traders find that the large majority are unprofitable after fees.
concept.misconceptions: That day trading is a form of investing or a reliable income source; the SEC states that day traders do not 'invest', typically suffer severe losses in their first months, and should never risk money needed for living expenses or retirement.
concept.example: A trader buys 500 shares of XYZ at $41.20 at 10:00 a.m. after a breakout, sells them at $41.75 by 11:30 a.m., and holds no position into the close.
